The greater one-horned rhinoceros exhibits substantial sexual dimorphism in body dimensions, with adult females reaching an ultimate body length of approximately 325 centimeters [Li = approximately 325 centimeters], whereas males are considerably larger, attaining a maximum body length ranging from 368 to 380 centimeters [Li = 368 to 380 centimeters]. Neonates are born after a gestation period that has been documented at 479 days [tg = 479 days] under the typical core body temperature of this species, which is 37.4 °C [T = 37.4 °C]. At birth, a newborn calf weighs roughly 58,000 grams [Wwb = roughly 58,000 grams], a substantial initial mass that reflects the precocial nature of the offspring. This considerable birth weight is critical for the calf's survival during the early postnatal period, as it must be able to stand and follow its mother within hours of delivery. The developmental trajectory of the young is closely tied to maternal investment during the lengthy suckling period.

The weaning process in the Indian rhinoceros marks a critical nutritional transition for the growing juvenile. Weaning occurs at 456 days after birth [tx = 456 days after birth] when maintained at the species' normal physiological temperature of 37.4 °C [T = 37.4 °C]. At this stage of dietary transition, the weanling has accumulated a substantial wet weight of approximately 885,812 grams [Wwx = approximately 885,812 grams], representing a remarkable increase from the neonatal mass. This nearly fifteen-fold increase in body mass over roughly fifteen months underscores the high milk production capacity of the lactating female and the rapid growth phase characteristic of this megaherbivore. The nutritional independence achieved at weaning allows the mother to redirect resources toward her own maintenance and potential future reproductive efforts, as the energetic demands of lactation are considerable for such a large-bodied mammal.

Under the thermoneutral conditions typical of the species, with a core body temperature of 37.4 °C [T = 37.4 °C], reproductive maturity in the greater one-horned rhinoceros is reached after an extended period of somatic growth. Puberty is attained at 1,678 days after birth [tp = 1,678 days after birth] at a temperature of 37.4 °C [T = 37.4 °C]. This protracted pre-reproductive juvenile phase, lasting roughly four and a half years, allows the sub-adult to achieve the considerable size necessary for successful competition and reproduction. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is approximately 1,602,330 grams [Wwi = approximately 1,602,330 grams], a figure that places the Indian rhinoceros among the largest of the extant terrestrial megaherbivores. This immense adult mass is the culmination of years of sustained feeding on a diet of grasses, shrubs, and aquatic vegetation within the floodplain ecosystems of the Indian subcontinent.

The maximum reproductive rate observed in the Indian rhinoceros reflects the species' notably slow life-history strategy. Females produce a single calf per reproductive event [N_R_i = single calf per reproductive event], with an average interval between births of approximately 850 days, yielding approximately 1 calf per 2.3 years [Ri = approximately 1 calf per 2.3 years], all measured at the species' typical core temperature of 37.4 °C [T = 37.4 °C]. This extended inter-birth interval is among the longest recorded for any ungulate and is consistent with the high degree of maternal investment required for each calf. The long gestation period and the prolonged lactation and juvenile dependency phase constrain the number of offspring a female can produce over her lifetime. Such a low fecundity makes the species particularly vulnerable to poaching and habitat loss, as population recovery from any decline is inherently slow.

Longevity records for the Indian rhinoceros indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 43.5 years [am = approximately 43.5 years] for individuals maintained under captive conditions at the species' typical core body temperature of 37.4 °C [T = 37.4 °C]. This considerable lifespan, combined with its late age at first reproduction and low annual reproductive output, defines a life-history strategy strongly oriented toward adult survival rather than high fecundity. Wild-living individuals likely experience reduced longevity due to the hazards of their environment, including predation on calves, territorial conflicts among adult males, and the pressures of habitat degradation. The demographic implications of this slow life-history pace are profound: populations require decades to recover from substantial losses, and the conservation of mature adults, particularly breeding females, is of paramount importance for the species' persistence across its remaining fragmented range.
